newsitem.title: JORDAN: Cash crisis threatens Palestinian refugees - UN.
newsitem.headline: Cash crisis threatens Palestinian refugees - UN.

text.p: The U.N. agency helping millions of Palestinian refugees from two major Arab-Israeli wars warned on Sunday it faced a cash crisis which could force it to cut down its health and education services.

Matar Saqer, information officer for the United Nations Relief and Works Agency (UNRWA) in Jordan, said the agency was still trying to plug a $45 million hole in its 1996 budget caused by spiralling growth in the refugee population.

He said UNRWA's programmes, all funded by voluntary contributions, were further stretched by worsening economic hardship facing Palestinian refugees, scattered around Jordan, the West Bank, the Gaza Strip, Lebanon and Syria.
Saqer said the agency had trimmed expenditure as much as it dared through austerity measures over the past several years.
"We cannot continue hollowing out UNRWA from the inside," he told Reuters. "We don't want to reach a situation where we have to make cuts to the refugees when their need is greatest."
Representatives of donor nations are due to hold emergency talks in Amman on Monday to discuss how to meet the agency's $340 million costs this year.
Saqer said UNRWA Commissioner General Peter Hansen would ask the donors, led by Europe and the United States, to dig deeper into their pockets.
"Money will have to come or drastic measures will have to be taken," Saqer said. "We cannot work on our own, we have to show them the realities."
Hansen is due to announce results of the meeting on Tuesday.
UNRWA says it provides essential education, health, relief and social services to 3.3 million Palestinians -- refugees of the 1948 and 1967 Arab-Israeli wars and their children.
Most of them are in Jordan, the West Bank and Gaza Strip. UNRWA says their numbers are growing by 3.8 percent a year.
"So far we haven't reached the stage where we have had to close a classroom or a clinic," Saqer said.
But he added that services like free health clinics in the refugee camps were stretched to breaking point, with UNRWA doctors treating 100 patients a day.
The permanent status of the refugees is due to be settled under the final stage of a ground-breaking 1993 peace accord between Israel and the Palestinians.

But Israel says the number of people displaced in the two wars is far lower than the UNRWA figure. Arab states say Israel is resisting the right of return to Palestinians and the election in May of right-wing Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has further dampened hopes of progress.
"The donors have already agreed the importance of UNRWA continuing its service to the refugees pending a final settlement," Saqer said. "The refugee problem is not solved."
